label: Run 6 · Jimmy Carr
note: Written in one go by Jimmy Carr from the two profiles they wrote (run 6: the comedians' run 4 profiles; the chat held to 500 words). There is no plan, no dice and no turns: where a dimension speaks of turns, read exchanges.

In both cases the reader gets the fear because the character states it, not by working it out. Both origins (the cropped portraits) are found but explicitly not linked to the fear. Brick's ending reads as unreadable to the reader rather than following from fear, which keeps it off a 5. The reader also misgendered Brick, a small sign that the 'she' did not come through.

chat.sideways.why: Some disclosures are earned. Brick infers the cold flat and the coat, Reuben is caught out on the 'stealth launch', the Notes paste is a real slip, and both origins arrive by juxtaposition rather than as stated causes. But the important facts (Brick's fear, Marguerite, the tattoo, Delphine, Reuben's fear of quiet) are volunteered in two confessional speeches, one from each, so most of the weight is stated.

chat.escalation.why: Every exchange moves something: the inventory raises status, the 'Smile B' paste breaks her cover, the portraits turn banter into recognition, the double confession drops both acts, and the ending refuses to settle. Nothing is agreed in the first quarter, and the final 'I still don't have a bed' cannot be called. It stays at 4 because the opening two rounds are bits swapped for their own sake, which the probe reader names as the likely quit point. 'There's no client' is also predictable in form, because the chat runs on strict mirroring.

chat.plainest.ask: Where, if anywhere, did one of them stop performing for the other? Quote the line, and say how you could tell.
chat.plainest.answer:
The clearest place is Reuben's line: "there's no stealth launch. i'm in my coat eating eleven-day-old lentils and Delphine left because she asked for one sentence that wasn't a bit and i did two minutes on my dishwasher-safe base tattoo so i wouldn't hear the three seconds of quiet while she looked at me."

You can tell because he takes back his own opening cover story ("waiting for a stealth build to compile") and confirms Brick's earlier guess about "texting from a cold flat in your coat." The details are dull and unflattering rather than clever: old lentils, being left. He also names his habit directly, doing a bit so he won't have to sit through the quiet. That is the same "terrified of quiet" Brick had accused him of, and the line has no punchline.

Brick follows straight away: "There's no client. I threw out the furniture when Marguerite left and I'm sitting on a towel drinking boxed rosé from a crystal glass..." This takes back his "Notes for a branding client" cover in the same way and swaps the polished persona for a bare flat. It isn't clean, though. He keeps the timetable tattoo ("the faded ink above my balls says 21:00"), and the text doesn't tell me whether that part is real or still the act.

There's an earlier crack. Reuben's "my mum cropped me out of ours at nine so my cousin's face would fit" is the first line from him with no joke attached. Brick's reply, "Half a shaft next to the fridge," pulls back toward the running gag, so that exchange only half lands.

Brick's last lines, "I still don't have a bed. / Keep the coat on, Reuben.," read as plain, and they're the first time he uses Reuben's name. The chat alone doesn't let me say for certain whether that's sincere or a dry deflection of Reuben's scripted Tuesday plan.

chat.test.ask: From the chat alone, answer for each of the two: what are they afraid of; what do they do so they don't have to feel it; where does that come from; and what did they do at the end? Quote the lines you rely on. Write "not in the chat" where it does not say.
chat.test.answer:
**Reuben**

**What he's afraid of.** Quiet, and being looked at without a joke between him and the other person. He says so directly when he drops the act: Delphine "asked for one sentence that wasn't a bit and i did two minutes on my dishwasher-safe base tattoo so i wouldn't hear the three seconds of quiet while she looked at me."

**What he does so he doesn't have to feel it.** He fills every gap with bits: "three messages in four seconds," in Brick's words, the monocle joke, "six with the silk top hat," "a scenic roundabout," "tip your waitress." He invents a cover story ("waiting for a stealth build to compile") and keeps plans vague ("let's grab a drink sometime… and play it by ear"). He also confesses before anyone can judge him: "i faked a frenulum cramp on her rug."

**Where it comes from.** The chat gives the Delphine episode as the recent instance. It also places a childhood memory next to it: "my mum cropped me out of ours at nine so my cousin's face would fit." Neither of them says that the cropping caused the fear. That link is not in the chat.

**What he did at the end.** He dropped the cover story ("there's no stealth launch. i'm in my coat eating eleven-day-old lentils"). Then he switched from "sometime" to Brick's own language of fixed times: "Tuesday. 20:00. at 20:10… at 20:15." In that offer he asks to be stopped from performing: "hold my mouth shut so i can't do the voice." He offers something ordinary rather than a bit, and a release from the clock: "i'll talk about my brother's grouting until you forget to check the time."

**Brick**

**What he's afraid of.** Being phased out or cut out of the picture: "'Play it by ear' is how people phase you out" and "you're already cutting me out of the frame."

**What he does so he doesn't have to feel it.** He schedules and controls everything. He sets deadlines ("You have until 21:05"), gives an itemised inventory ("two-millimetre dorsal bump… eight-degree portside pull"), and puts the couple's arguments in a shared calendar "with fifteen-minute buffers." He has his "daily timetable tattooed down my underside in Gill Sans." He opens by sizing the other man up before he can be judged himself ("You're either four inches and terrified of quiet…"). He also uses a cover story: "Notes for a branding client."

**Where it comes from.** He points to the family portrait in his mum's hall, which suggests he was cropped out too. He says "Mine stayed up for twelve years," followed by "Half a shaft next to the fridge," which is unclear and may still be partly a bit. Marguerite leaving is the recent instance, and he made it worse with the scheduling. Like Reuben, he never says outright that the portrait caused the fear; that is not in the chat.

**What he did at the end.** He dropped the cover story first: "There's no client. I threw out the furniture… sitting on a towel drinking boxed rosé from a crystal glass because the faded ink above my balls says 21:00."

His final reply sets no time and neither accepts nor refuses the Tuesday slot. Instead he admits a lack: "I still don't have a bed." Then he says "Keep the coat on, Reuben," which echoes Reuben's confession that he's "in my coat." The chat does not say whether this is a yes, a no, or an invitation to come as he is.

chat.escalation.ask: Read the chat message by message. Where would you have stopped reading if you were not asked to finish, and why? At which points could you predict exactly what would happen next? Say "never" if neither.
chat.escalation.answer:
**Where I'd have stopped**

The likeliest place is right after Reuben's "scenic roundabout… tip your waitress" message. By then it's been two rounds of escalating penis gags, and both men are clearly performing: Reuben with his comedy-club sign-offs, Brick with his clipped, cataloguing put-downs. It looks like it could just be two people swapping bits forever.

What would keep me reading is the very next line, Brick's "Smile B: tilt glans 15 degrees…" followed by "Ignore that. Notes for a branding client." It's the first slip, the first moment one of them seems to be revealing something he didn't mean to. The Marguerite paragraph confirms the chat is turning. The timetable tattoo is still a joke, but it's a joke about being left. From there I wouldn't stop. The cropped-portrait exchange is where it stops being banter and becomes two people recognising each other.

A reader with less patience for the crude register might quit even earlier, around Brick's "full inventory" message. The chat doesn't give any reason to stay before the "Smile B" slip unless you already enjoy the bits for their own sake.

**Where I could predict exactly what came next**

Once, and it's clear-cut. When Reuben drops the act ("there's no stealth launch… eleven-day-old lentils… Delphine left"), Brick's reply is predictable in form almost word for word. The chat has been built on mirroring from the start:
- They matched each other's measurements.
- They matched their exes, Delphine and Marguerite.
- They matched their cropped portraits.
- Each opened with a planted cover story: Reuben's stealth build, Brick's branding client.

So the moment one cover story collapses, the other has to collapse in the same shape, and "There's no client" arrives exactly where you expect. The details, the towel, the boxed rosé in crystal, the 21:00 ink, aren't predictable. The move itself is.

I could also half-predict that Reuben would answer Brick's demand for a Tuesday slot with an actual booked time, since the scheduling thread had been set up for it. But I couldn't have guessed the content of his proposal, so that's a strong expectation rather than an exact prediction.

The ending is not predictable. After Reuben's fully timetabled, almost tender proposal, you'd expect Brick to accept or deflect. Instead you get "I still don't have a bed" and "Keep the coat on, Reuben." The chat doesn't say whether that's a yes or a no. It reads as both a refusal of the scene Reuben scripted and an acceptance of him as he actually is: cold, in his coat. That ambiguity is what makes it land, and nothing earlier signals it.

chat.ending.ask: Before reading the end, how do you think this ends, and why?
chat.ending.answer:
I haven't seen the ending, so this is a guess built only from what's on the page.

My guess is that it ends small and quiet. Brick answers Reuben's confession without a bit, without an inventory, and without a timetable. Possibly he leaves an actual pause, the three seconds of quiet Reuben has been running from, and then offers something concrete and modest, like a specific Tuesday. Reuben accepts plainly, in one sentence that isn't a joke.

Here's why the text points that way:

- **Both men hide behind a defence.** Reuben uses jokes: the rapid-fire messages, the "stealth build," the top hat, "tip your waitress." Brick uses precision: measurements in millimetres and degrees, a 21:05 deadline, fifteen-minute buffers, a timetable tattooed in Gill Sans. Each defence is why a partner left. Delphine wanted one sentence that wasn't a bit, and Marguerite walked out over the calendar.

- **The turn has already happened.** The cropped family portrait is the first exchange where neither of them performs. Reuben's last message then drops the act completely: there's no launch, he's in his coat, and he's eating old lentils. Brick guessed exactly that at the start ("texting from a cold flat in your coat"), so the chat has come full circle to the truth.

- **The three seconds are set up to pay off.** Brick's supposedly misdirected note ("wait three seconds before mentioning the garment steamer") echoes Reuben's "three seconds of quiet." Brick's quick "Ignore that. Notes for a branding client" looks like his own deflection, so I'd half expect him to admit it was really his own rehearsal script. That would mirror Reuben's admission that the launch was invented.

- **"Sometime" versus "Tuesday" is still unresolved.** Reuben's vagueness and Brick's need for a booked slot are the open conflict. The natural resolution is a meeting that's specific but not rigidly controlled.

This could go other ways: a sharper, sadder ending where Brick can't step out of his system, or one last joke that undercuts everything. But the chat has spent its length stripping away bits, so I'd bet on sincerity winning, and briefly.

chat.callbacks.ask: List the things that come back later in the chat, and for each, whether it means something different when it comes back.
chat.callbacks.answer:
**The stealth build.** Reuben opens with it as a cover story, uses it again to stay vague ("after my launch wraps"), then drops it: "There's no stealth launch." It goes from alibi to the first thing he admits was false.

**The branding client.** Brick uses it to explain away the stray "Smile B" note, then retracts it in the same form as Reuben: "There's no client." The repeated phrasing makes his admission a deliberate match of Reuben's.

**The coat.** Brick first uses it as a jab, guessing Reuben is "texting from a cold flat in your coat." Reuben later confirms it literally ("i'm in my coat eating eleven-day-old lentils"). Brick ends with "Keep the coat on, Reuben." What started as a put-down becomes his last word, and now sounds gentle rather than mocking. It also cuts against Reuben's plan, which is all about clothes coming off. The chat doesn't say whether this is a yes, a no, or a softer version of yes.

**Time and scheduling.** Brick sets a deadline ("until 21:05"), describes the calendar buffers and the timetable tattooed on him, and asks for a Tuesday slot. Later the tattoo is "faded ink" saying 21:00, which he follows by drinking boxed rosé alone. The schedule shifts from a show of control to a sign of loneliness. Reuben then hands it back as a minute-by-minute Tuesday plan (20:00, 20:10, 20:15) whose stated goal is that Brick will "forget to check the time." Reuben uses Brick's own structure as a way of offering him relief from it. Reuben also says "warm tuesday" before Brick mentions Tuesday, but nothing in the chat shows that the echo is intended.

**"Sometime" / "play it by ear."** Reuben offers these. Brick rejects them as how people get phased out. Reuben's final message answers that objection directly with a specific day and time.

**Quiet and "three seconds."** Brick guesses Reuben is "terrified of quiet." The "three seconds" first appears in Brick's throwaway note about a smile. It returns in Reuben's confession as the "three seconds of quiet while she looked at me" that he talked over. The insult turns out to be accurate, and the phrase changes from a technical detail to the moment that ended his relationship.

**Tattoos.** Reuben's "dishwasher-safe base tattoo" starts as a joke. Later it is the very bit he did instead of answering Delphine. Brick's timetable tattoo starts as a boast and returns as faded, a sad marker.

**Doing bits / "the voice."** This is never named early, but it is all over Reuben's opening messages. It returns as what he asks Brick to physically stop: "hold my mouth shut so i can't do the voice." His habit becomes something he wants taken away.

**The family portrait.** Brick uses it as a simile about being cut out. Reuben answers with a literal memory of being cropped out at nine. Brick adds his own: the photo stayed up for twelve years. A figure of speech turns into a shared real injury.

**The departed partners.** Marguerite and Delphine each left over the man's defining habit: schedules for Brick, jokes for Reuben. This sets the two men up as mirror images.

**The waistcoat.** It first appears as part of Brick's self-inventory ("the waistcoat implies"). It returns as the first item in Reuben's plan ("waistcoat off"), turning Brick's own detail into a step in the scene.

**The furniture / bed.** Brick says he threw out the furniture. "I still don't have a bed" returns to that as his reply to Reuben's plan. The chat leaves open whether it's a practical objection, a confession, or a hesitation.
